findings.issue: "700 graph inputs for cut-vertex/bridge checks" comes right after the sentence on independent oracles, so it reads as 700 oracle comparisons. Only seeds 1-400 are compared against the brute force that removes a vertex or edge and recounts components. Seeds 401-700 check only the root rule, against the run's own parent map, with no oracle. The report's own source [7] lists "seeds 1-400" for this oracle.
findings.evidence: visualgo-plus-design@662e7b3 prototypes/src/graph/algorithms/cutVertexBridge/cutVertexBridgeProperty.test.ts:81-121: seeds 1..400 are checked against bruteForce() (:66-73, component recount at :45-64). Lines :123-140: seeds 401..700 assert childCount against last.parentByNodeId and cutVertexIds.includes(root) === childCount >= 2 only. docsforfyp 04_figures_and_validation.md:176 lists "seeds 1-400 ... brute force". 02_contribution_evidence.md:98 says "400 seeds ... + 300 seeds". The other two counts are right: Bellman-Ford uses 2 x 70 = 140 fixtures (createBellmanFordSequence.test.ts:241-262) and Prim uses 20 fixtures x every start (primEngine.test.ts:258-302).
findings.fix: Reword to: "The recorded randomized cases include 400 random multigraphs compared with the removal oracle (plus 300 more that check the root rule), 140 signed graphs for Bellman–Ford, and 20 small graphs for Prim tested from every start vertex."

findings.section: 4.6 Graph extensions and algorithm validation, paragraph 1
findings.issue: "The traversal interface also supports an End node where applicable" does not say which algorithms have it. Only BFS, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford take an End node. It is a shortest-path query whose path is drawn on the run's last frame (DD-45). The DFS variants, Topological Sort, Bipartite Check and Cut Vertex & Bridge have none, and two of the three algorithms that do are shortest-path algorithms, not traversals.
findings.evidence: prototypes/src/graph/algorithms/shortestPathQuery.ts:11 defines ShortestPathAlgorithmId = 'bfs' | 'dijkstra' | 'bellman-ford', and :53-60 holds the set and supportsShortestPathQuery. prototypes/src/graph/components/panels/AlgorithmRunForm.tsx:138-141 renders the "End node" select only when supportsShortestPathQuery(algorithmId) is true. The control is visible as "END NODE All vertices" in Figures 3, 4 and 8 (F2/F3/F4 PNGs).
findings.fix: Suggested wording: "BFS, Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford also accept an optional End node; the final frame then draws the shortest path to it (DD-45)."

positives: The 11 graph algorithm ids and the Method options (topological sort: DFS/Kahn; bipartite: DFS/BFS) match the registry exactly: prototypes/src/graph/algorithms/algorithmIntegration.ts:137-210 and algorithmMethods.ts:36-51.

The parallel-edge paragraph matches the code. The parent edge is skipped by edge id (createCutVertexBridgeSequence.ts:169-175), and any other edge to the parent vertex is treated as a back edge (:197-223). The unit test createCutVertexBridgeSequence.test.ts:118-138 and the e2e test graph-traversal.spec.ts:402-421 (CP4 4.22) both cover it.

The oracle descriptions are accurate. Cut Vertex & Bridge is checked by removing a vertex or edge and recounting components (cutVertexBridgeProperty.test.ts:45-73). Bellman-Ford is checked against a Floyd-Warshall all-pairs oracle that includes negative-cycle reachability (createBellmanFordSequence.test.ts:223-262). Prim is checked by exhaustive edge-subset search (primEngine.test.ts:51-77). The 140 and 20-from-every-start counts are right.

The Figure 5 values are correct. I recomputed them by hand from CP3_4_9 (visualgoExamples.ts:90-98); they match the PNG, including the num,low badges, and graph-traversal.spec.ts:354-376 asserts them.

The 'witnesses' claim holds. The DFS topological sort stops on a cycle (createTopologicalSortDfsSteps.ts:131-140). Kahn ends by listing the stuck vertices, each with indegree above zero, which is a valid certificate of a cycle (createKahnSteps.ts:125-142). Both bipartite methods stop on an odd cycle (createBipartiteCheckDfsSteps.ts:132-140, createBipartiteCheckBfsSteps.ts:120-128).

The captions of Figures 3, 4 and 7 match their PNGs: Frame 8/22 in the default layout; the drag preview with the framed Pseudocode group, ghost label and dashed bottom band; Merge/Bubble/Quick/Radix at size 48.

The tree and sorting claims are verified. There are seven workspaces (src/tree/app/workspaceModes.ts:14-22). The catalogs hold the BST queries, traversals, AVL Delete and nine heap operations. The lazy segment tree's Range Update is a range add (createLazyRangeUpdateSequence.ts:19-29), and the heap has a preview with Apply (HeapMode.tsx:49). Sorting has 1/2/4 panes for Study and Compare (sortingCatalog.ts:5-9). Duplicate panes are disabled (useSortingExperiment.ts:373-381). The randomized quicksort pivot is seeded from the dataset seed (comparisonSorts.ts:277-285, useSortingExperiment.ts:262).
The hedging in sections 4.6-4.7 is appropriate and should stay: 'not a formal proof', 'a playback coordinate, not a measurement of relative runtime', 'do not imply complete operation parity'.

findings.issue:
The timing paragraph is wrong in three places.
1. 'Notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds': the 200 ms floor applies to the note's remaining display time, which is 90% of the step interval. A 200 ms step therefore gets no note; the first interval that shows one is about 223 ms.
2. 'Limited by the step interval and configured delay': step notes have no delay, because the writer always sets delayMs to 0. The only setting involved is Speed, which together with the step's pace gives the interval.
3. 'A manually inspected note': notes appear only when a step is reached one step forward (Next or autoplay). Previous, First, Last and the scrubber show none.

This matters for the section's own example. At the default 0.5 s speed during autoplay, a rejected Dijkstra relaxation ('· keep') note shows for about 0.3 s, and an 'already settled' note does not show at all.

findings.issue: MISMATCH: 'During autoplay, its duration is limited by the step interval and configured delay; notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds' misstates the code. During autoplay a note lasts min(1,600 ms, 0.9 x step interval - delay), and it is dropped when that result is under 200 ms. Step notes are always created with delay 0, so they disappear when the step interval is below about 222 ms, not 200 ms, and no configured delay applies to them. The evidence pack states this correctly (doc 02 line 122); the report's paraphrase lost the 0.9 factor. The 1,600 ms life when stepping by hand is a MATCH.

findings.section: 1.1 Project background; 2.3 Position of this work
findings.issue: There is no explicit problem statement. Section 1.1 gives only the supervisor's direction to modernize the Laravel/PHP, MySQL, D3 and jQuery stack. It never says what is wrong with that stack or with the current interface, who the users are, or what problem the rebuild solves for them. The report's real problem formulation, the three design questions, sits at the end of Background (p.3, after the objectives). It is linked only as a block to 'Sections 4.2-4.8', although 4.3, 4.6 and 4.7 answer none of the three questions.
findings.evidence: report/main.tex:62-67 (section 1.1); main.tex:108 (the three design questions). In report-pages.txt the word 'problem' occurs only on p.11 (line 516) and p.13 (line 610), and 'objective' only in the section 1 heading and 1.3. No target audience or course is named anywhere ('learner/student' appears on 10 lines of main.tex, never with a definition). Bao's own records already document the three problems. (P1) graph-visualizer-v2 docs/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:7-37 (DD-01/DD-02, commit 0f5b49a, 2026-08-30): V1 'couples a large App, local editor state, Edit/Run modes, graph snapshots, and two canvas branches'; 'Separate render branches previously diverged in node/edge types, markers, viewport behavior, and edge visibility'. (P2) design/proposals/viz-shell-v10/README.md:124-128: 'V2 keeps every panel in a fixed place and lets several be open at once; V7 lets the visitor rearrange the panels but shows only one tab per dock'. (P3) prototypes/docs/tree/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:2683-2701 (TP-34, 2026-10-23): text 'right on the canvas instead of showing too much in Status, especially the dead steps'. The official NUS SoC CA Main Evaluator form (FYP-CA-1910-revised-2024-0120.pdf, Table 1) lists 'Formulation and problem statement' under 'Understanding of the problem (30%)'; its top band reads 'Good formulation of the problem statement with clear and viable objectives'.
findings.fix: Insert a short '1.2 Problem statement' before the objectives (about 150 words), and move the personal motivation after it or shorten it (see PU-7). Draft: 'VisuAlgo+ serves [owner: audience, e.g. students in introductory data-structures courses and self-learners]. VisuAlgo's stack (Laravel/PHP, MySQL, D3, jQuery) [owner: the supervisor's reason, e.g. makes new visualizations costly to add and maintain]. Rebuilding the visualizers raised three problems. P1, editing vs playback: in my first prototype, separate Edit and Run canvases diverged in node and edge types, markers, viewport and edge visibility, so an edit could disagree with the run on screen [V2 DD-01, DD-02]. P2, one page for different topics: split rails (V2) kept every panel visible but fixed, while docks (V7) let panels move but showed one tab per dock [V10 proposal section 1]. P3, silent steps: many steps change state without visible motion, such as a rejected Dijkstra relaxation, and were explained only in the Status panel, away from the edge [TP-34].' Then map them explicitly: P1 -> 4.2, P2 -> 4.4-4.5, P3 -> 4.8. In 2.3, keep the three questions only as a back-reference.
findings.confirmation_question: What reason did A/P Halim give for leaving the Laravel/PHP + jQuery stack (maintainability, extensibility, engine reuse, something else)? Who is VisuAlgo+'s target audience (which courses or users)?

findings.evidence: VERIFIED: sentence counts by a script over report-pages.txt, pages 1-14. The learning/usability caveat appears on p.1 (main.tex:51), p.2 (:88), p.3 (:96, :101), p.4 (:117), p.11 (:275), p.12 (:300) and p.13 (twice). findings.fix: State the limits once: the full list in 6.2 and one sentence in the abstract. Delete: main.tex:101 sentences 3-4 ('It does not establish... Those claims require evaluation...'); main.tex:117 sentence 2; main.tex:275 sentence 1; main.tex:300 sentence 3 ('The counts also reflect test organization...'); and the abstract's 'These results support functional progress.' Abstract draft: 'VisuAlgo+ rebuilds VisuAlgo on a modern web foundation while keeping its educational purpose. A faithful rebuild must solve three problems: edits that can disagree with the run on screen, topics that need different panels in one consistent page, and steps that change state without visible motion. I built the graph, tree and sorting visualizers and their integration: separate state owners so that editing and playback share one canvas; the V10 panel-group layout, a pure model with checked invariants used by all three visualizers; algorithm extensions validated with randomized oracle tests; and floating text that explains a step beside its node or edge, informed by a Week 10 user trial. On 1 November 2026, 3,273 unit tests and 151 browser cases passed; learning effects, usability and performance are not yet measured. Next: browser tests for panel interactions, a task-based evaluation and one engine-integration slice with Kerk.' Use the space saved for PU-1 and PU-2.

findings.issue: The literature is relevant but dated: the only scholarly sources are from 2002-2012, and the rest are web pages or library docs. None of it addresses the two design questions behind Bao's central contributions. Design question 3 (an explanation placed away from the drawing forces the learner to 'look away') is the well-studied split-attention / spatial-contiguity problem, yet it is argued without a source. The interaction model V10 follows (VS Code-style editor groups) is never named.
findings.evidence: References: [2] 2012, [3] 2002, [5] 2010; [4], [1] and [9] are web documentation (report-pages.txt:706-728). main.tex:265 argues 'the learner must repeatedly look away from the relevant edge' without a citation. 'VS Code' does not occur in main.tex (grep), while the V10 brief says 'Like VS Code, but with a canvas' (design/proposals/viz-shell-v10/README.md:45). On the CA form, the sub-criterion 'Literature survey and review of previous works' (top band: 'up-to-date and critical') sits under 'Understanding of the problem (30%)'. Two suggested citations, checked on the web: Chandler & Sweller (1991), Cognition and Instruction 8(4):293-332, doi:10.1207/s1532690xci0804_2; Naps et al. (2002), 'Exploring the role of visualization and engagement in computer science education', ACM SIGCSE Bulletin 35(2):131-152, doi:10.1145/960568.782998.
findings.fix: In 2.1 or 4.8, cite the split-attention effect (Chandler & Sweller 1991, or Mayer's spatial-contiguity principle) as the reason for placing explanations beside the edge, and keep the statement that VisuAlgo+'s own effect is unmeasured. In 2.1, add Naps et al. 2002's engagement taxonomy next to Hundhausen [3]: it turns 'how learners used AV' into levels (viewing, changing input, responding) that can frame Table 4's tasks. In 2.3, name VS Code's editor groups as the interaction model V10 follows, as a design reference rather than a research claim. If space allows, add one post-2015 study of algorithm-visualization effectiveness.

The user-side problem behind design question 3 is therefore asserted rather than shown.

TP-34 (prototypes/docs/tree/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:2688-2701, 2026-10-23) states the design problem precisely: 'instead of showing too much in Status, especially the dead steps, the ones that change nothing on the visualization'.

If the footage has only been viewed informally, say so ('informal review; systematic coding is the first follow-up step, 6.3') and state the design problem in TP-34's terms (steps that change nothing on the drawing were explained only in Status), which the trial reinforced. findings.confirmation_question: What did the Week 10 recordings show that led to floating text? For example, did participants look to Status, or get lost, on steps where nothing moved? If the footage has not been analysed yet, may the report say it was reviewed informally?

positives: The five objectives are explicitly enumerated on p.2, and objective 5 builds evaluation into the project.
The three design questions in 2.3 (p.3) are a sharp, project-specific problem formulation. Promote and link them rather than rewrite them.
The scope is honest: 'an experimental application, not yet a full replacement', and 'The separate WebAssembly engine has not been connected' (p.2).

The report is strongly aware of its own shortcomings and pairs each with a proposed next step: eager timelines, unbounded sorting history, note overlap and untested drag/split lead to 6.4 and Tables 4-5. This matches the top band of the official 'Issues, constraints and assumptions' sub-criterion.
The distinction between correctness and understanding drawn from Hundhausen et al. (p.3) is a sound frame for the evaluation plan.
Kerk is named on p.2, and the joint V10 decisions (choices 27-48) are credited in 3.2, consistent with the owner's recorded answers (doc 01, Q3).
7.1 names scope growth as the main project risk and proposes prioritizing the existing graph, tree and sorting workflows, which shows good judgement.

findings.issue: The sorting limitation sentence is wrong in two ways. (1) History is never trimmed, but it is not unbounded: every input is capped at 240 values, and a code comment records the worst-case size. (2) 'Distant seeks can require substantial replay' gets the cost model wrong. A backward seek always replays from a fresh state up to the target, so its cost grows with the target's position, not with how far the seek jumps. In addition, at the app's input sizes the 60,000-operation priming usually holds the whole comparison, so the lazy path only matters for the largest combinations.
findings.evidence: docsforfyp report/main.tex:195, and :312 ('Sorting retains unbounded history'). visualgo-plus-design prototypes/src/sorting/app/useSortingExperiment.ts:25 sets MAX_CUSTOM_VALUES = 240, enforced on the resolved input at :90-91. Bao's comment above EAGER_OPERATION_CAP (src/sorting/comparison/operationBuffer.ts:232-246, from 5ccef45) records counts: shipped 4-pane default at n=48 = 3,356 operations; n=160 = 25,015; n=240 = 53,034; worst 4-pane choice at n=240 = 159,298; 105-180 bytes per operation. Priming runs to 60,000 summed across panes (:292-327). For a backward seek, seekComparison calls replayOperations(input, run.history.slice(0, consumed)) (src/sorting/comparison/comparisonPlayback.ts:346-352). replayOperations is applySortOperations(createPlaybackState(input), operations) (src/sorting/engine/operations.ts:446-451). A one-step Previous instead reverts a single operation (retreatComparison, comparisonPlayback.ts:257-300).
findings.fix: Replace the second sentence at main.tex:195 with, for example: 'However, retained history is never trimmed. It is bounded only by the 240-value input cap (about 159,000 operations in the largest four-pane case, by a count recorded in the code). A backward seek replays every retained operation from the start to the target, so seeks late in a long run cost the most. At the app's input sizes the 60,000-operation priming usually holds the whole comparison; the lazy path matters only for the largest combinations.' Change main.tex:312 to match ('Sorting never trims its history and replays it when seeking backwards').

findings.issue: Section 2 reads as a set of one-source summaries, each followed by a caveat about VisuAlgo+, not as a review organised around the report's own design questions. Its peer-reviewed base is three papers, the newest from 2012. Two of the three design questions in 2.3 (shared layout across topics; explaining steps with little visible motion) have no supporting literature, and neither has the evaluation plan in 6.3.
findings.evidence: References (p15): the peer-reviewed sources are [2] 2012, [3] 2002 and [5] 2010; [4] is a web page; [1] and [9] are library documentation; [6]-[8] are own notes. External citations appear only on pp. 2-3. Sections 4.4 (V10), 4.8 (floating text) and 6.3-6.4 cite no external source. The three design questions come only after the literature (p3, main.tex:108), and none of [2]-[5] addresses layout or on-canvas explanation. The evidence pack itself lists seven 'Topics that need external literature' (docsforfyp/05_report_mapping_and_questions.md:87-96): AV evaluation; step animation and explanations on the drawing; layout and docking; force and tidy-tree layout; test oracles; WebAssembly; accessibility. The report covers topic 1 with literature and topic 4 only with docs. The NUS SoC 'Submission Guidelines for CA Report' (comp.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/FYP_CA_Report_Guidlines_Oct_22.pdf) require a literature review and point to the U of Toronto advice. That advice says a review must be 'organized around and related directly to the thesis or research question', is 'not just a descriptive list ... or a set of summaries', and 'It's usually a bad sign to see every paragraph beginning with the name of a researcher.' Three of the five paragraphs in 2.1-2.2 open with the source's name (main.tex:94, 98, 101). None of the caveats assesses a source's own strengths or weaknesses. For example, the report never notes that Halim et al. 2012's evidence is a self-report survey of 31 students (24 CS3233 + 7 CS2020; 'More than half ... reported enhancement ... the other half reported neutral impact', pp. 65-67 of the paper).

(a) Naps T.L., Rossling G., Almstrum V., Dann W., Fleischer R., Hundhausen C., Korhonen A., Malmi L., McNally M., Rodger S., Velazquez-Iturbide J.A. 2002. Exploring the role of visualization and engagement in computer science education. ITiCSE-WGR '02, ACM, 131-152. doi:10.1145/960568.782998 (also SIGCSE Bulletin 35(2), 2003, doi:10.1145/782941.782998). Its engagement taxonomy fits question 3 and the follow-up tasks.
(b) Chandler P., Sweller J. 1991. Cognitive load theory and the format of instruction. Cognition and Instruction 8(4):293-332. doi:10.1207/s1532690xci0804_2. The split-attention effect is the stated rationale for floating text (4.8).
(c) Wang Baldonado M.Q., Woodruff A., Kuchinsky A. 2000. Guidelines for using multiple views in information visualization. AVI '00, 110-119. doi:10.1145/345513.345271. It fits question 2 and V10: the drawing, pseudocode, Status and array strip are coordinated views of one step.
(d) Halim S. 2015. VisuAlgo - Visualising data structures and algorithms through animation. Olympiads in Informatics 9:243-245. doi:10.15388/ioi.2015.20 (see LIT-4).

findings.issue: Hundhausen et al. [3] is cited accurately, but only to separate 'does the software behave correctly' from 'do students learn'. The report never applies the paper's central result: what learners do matters more than what they see. That result bears directly on the main post-trial feature (floating text, which learners only view), on input editing (a what-if activity) and on the planned follow-up tasks.
findings.evidence: [3] abstract (faculty.cc.gatech.edu/~stasko/papers/jvlc02.pdf, text extracted): 'a systematic meta-study of 24 experimental studies ... Our most significant finding is that how students use AV technology has a greater impact on effectiveness than what AV technology shows them.' The p3 paraphrase is faithful. Section 6.3 of the paper (p. 284): 'studies in which students merely viewed visualizations did not demonstrate significant learning advantages over students who used conventional learning materials'. The successful uses it names engage students in 'what-if analyses', 'prediction exercises' and 'programming exercises'. Section 6.2: 'procedural knowledge may serve as a more sensitive measure ... than conceptual knowledge'. Pre/post improvement is more sensitive, but 'the pre-test may give participants knowledge of the target algorithm'. In the report, p3 (main.tex:96) uses [3] only for the two-questions split. Section 4.8 (p11) presents floating text as reducing attention switching, and Table 4 (p14) plans 'Correct prediction of the next swap' and explanation tasks; neither refers back to [3].
findings.fix: Add 2-3 sentences to 2.1, e.g.: 'The meta-study's evidence favours what learners do (what-if analyses, predictions) over what they see [3]. VisuAlgo+'s input editing supports what-if exploration; floating text is a viewing aid, so its value has to be tested with an active task.' Add a one-line cross-reference in 4.8. In 6.3, label the Table 4 tasks by Naps et al.'s engagement levels (predict/explain = responding; edit input or rearrange = changing). Note [3]'s measurement advice: prefer procedural tasks, and watch for the pre-test effect if you use a pre/post design. Minor precision: write '24 controlled experiments' rather than '24 studies'.

findings.issue: The report says Halim et al. 2012 'present VisuAlgo', but that paper never uses the name. The source that does name VisuAlgo (Halim 2015) also documents VisuAlgo's Online Quiz. It also lists '(4) ... accessible on modern portable PCs including tablets and smartphones'. [5] Shaffer et al. 2010 lists all seven authors in the right order, with TOCE 10(3) Article 9 (9:1-9:22) and a valid DOI; all of this matches the ACM reference line printed in the paper. 'Availability, quality and topic coverage' is a fair summary of its abstract.

crit-management.notes:
VERDICT (Project Management): The report clearly shows meaningful, well-evidenced Semester 1 progress. The management story around that progress is under-presented, and the Semester 2 plan is not yet realistic as written. Main gaps: (1) Table 5 schedules the final-report writing after the published deadline (Wed 7 Apr 2027) and leaves out the CA presentation and the exams; (2) the Week 10 trial is a vague claim with no dates, count or concrete observation; (3) no challenge is described as a problem overcome, and no slip is reflected on, although the repository has good examples; (4) Table 1 cannot be mapped to NUS weeks; (5) dependencies on Kerk, the risks and the ethics step are generic or missing. Suggested order before 17:00: PM-1, PM-2 (needs Bao's numbers), PM-4, PM-3, then PM-5, PM-6 and PM-7 as short additions. Estimated effort 1-1.5 hours. Page budget: the SoC CA guidelines say 10-15 pages (VERIFIED, FYP_CA_Report_Guidlines_Oct_22.pdf). The PDF has 16 pages including the title page and a back-matter page, and p.13 has about a third of a page free, so additions should be offset, e.g. by shortening 6.2's first paragraph and the 4.6 parallel-edge paragraph.
COULD NOT CHECK: The criteria tables on the CA evaluation form (comp.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/CA-Evaluation-Form.pdf) are images. The text layer shows only that each form 'counts 15% towards the final grade', plus the feedback headings 'Work done and amount of effort invested so far', 'Areas of weakness' and 'What is expected at the end of the project'. The claimed 10-20% weight for project management is therefore unverified. I also could not check: the Week 10 recordings, participant count, dates and consent; Kerk's survey data; the current NUS-IRB and SoC rules for FYP user studies; and whether the supervisor has seen the plan. I read the SoC FYP page through WebFetch summaries (two fetches, consistent with each other). I read the calendar from the registrar's own PDF via pdftotext.
SIDE OBSERVATIONS FOR OTHER REVIEWERS: (a) The registrar calendar confirms that Week 1 began on Mon 10 Aug 2026, which closes evidence-pack Q1. (b) p.4 says Kerk's survey informed 'the choice between the V2 split-rail and V7 dock-based layouts', whereas the owner's Q8 answer (doc 01 line 25) says V2 and V7 were chosen after the survey. Choosing between the two is not the same as choosing the two out of nine, so confirm the wording with the owner. (c) 'DRAFT FOR REVIEW' (main.tex:48) and the 'Draft' running header (main.tex:27) are still in the PDF; remove them before submission (report/README.md:38). I edited no file in either repository.

findings.issue: The report never states its central technical contribution as a few positive claims that a reader can check. The abstract lists topics ('This report explains the separation of input, layout and playback state; the V10 panel-group model; ...'). §2.3 says the value 'lies in connecting them coherently' and disclaims novelty, §3.2 lists areas of work, and §4 opens with a box diagram. The hard parts and what the design guarantees are scattered across pp. 6–11, surrounded by disclaimers. Those guarantees: a run survives layout edits but not semantic edits; stale timer events are ignored; the drop preview equals the committed layout; results stay correct on multigraphs; notes are placed in screen space and timed to playback speed. An evaluator has to piece the achievement together.
findings.evidence: report-pages.txt lines 34-36 (abstract), 143-146 (§2.3), 203-208 (§3.2), 228-231 (§4.1). A grep for 'does not|cannot|not a/an/yet/evidence/claimed…' matches 31 lines. Each suggested claim below checks out at 662e7b3: prototypes/src/graph/visualization/sessionReducer.ts:36-38, 100-104, 168-171 (topology-changed ends a run; a tick counts only with the same sessionId); prototypes/src/shared/components/layout/groupsModel.test.ts:1220, 1252-1254 (4,000-step walk; the released state toStrictEqual the dropTransition result); prototypes/src/graph/algorithms/cutVertexBridge/createCutVertexBridgeSequence.ts:169-170 (parent edge skipped by id); prototypes/src/shared/visualization/stepNotePlacement.ts:1-9 and floatingTextTiming.ts:27-30; prototypes/src/sorting/comparison/operationBuffer.ts:246, 285-296; wasm-arch/engine/src/session.cc:154 ('first occurrence wins for parallel edges').
findings.fix: Add a 5–6 line paragraph, 'Technical contributions this semester', at the start of §4 (p.5), and echo its first sentence in the abstract. Make no novelty claim; each item should be checkable. Suggested items: (1) A run model for editable graphs. A run is an immutable typed step sequence built from a revisioned document; layout edits never invalidate it, semantic edits always do, and timer ticks from an older run are ignored (§4.2). (2) Edge identity as part of the meaning. Parallel edges and self-loops stay distinct in every algorithm. This keeps cut-vertex/bridge results correct on multigraphs and is the first requirement for engine integration, because the engine prototype currently looks edges up by their endpoints. (3) V10 as a pure layout model that keeps its invariants. One resolver serves sizing, drop validity, preview and commit, and a 4,000-step seeded random walk checks after every step that the preview equals the released layout and that every invariant holds (§4.4). (4) A shared note layer drawn in screen space, with placement that avoids obstacles and timing that follows playback speed, used by both the graph and tree visualizers (§4.8). (5) A sorting player that keeps one to four lazy operation streams on one clock and seeks exactly by replay (§4.3). (6) Six added graph algorithms and 36 tree operation identifiers across seven workspaces, checked against independent oracles (§4.6–4.7). Then let §6 state the limitations once instead of repeating disclaimers through §4.

findings.section: §4.3 Sorting uses a different execution model
findings.issue: An evaluator cannot follow the sorting execution model as written, and parts of it mislead. (1) 'Operation' is never defined. (2) 'primes streams up to a 60,000-operation aggregate threshold' omits why priming exists (so the scrubber's end is exact) and that the cap is summed across panes and spent round robin (so histories stay level). It also omits that every run at the default size is therefore produced whole, so 'This approach avoids requiring every sort to finish generating before interaction begins' is true only for large inputs. (3) 'Common operation index' is not defined: each pane shows min(tick, its length) operations. (4) 'Retained history remains unbounded' omits that input sizes are capped (160 generated values, 240 custom). The code's own note puts the worst run at about 159,000 operations.

SortOperation is a union of 9 kinds (compare, swap, write, pivot, markSorted, auxWrite, bucket push/collect, phase). prototypes/docs/sorting/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:159-202 (SP-05, SP-06). prototypes/src/sorting/comparison/seekComparison.test.ts:69, 83, 94. findings.fix: Rewrite §4.3 in about eight sentences, for example: 'Each sorting algorithm is a generator that yields typed operations (compare, swap, write, pivot, mark-sorted, and bucket or auxiliary writes for counting and radix sort) instead of array snapshots. One clock drives every pane: at tick t a pane has applied min(t, its length) operations to its own copy of the shared input, so a pane that finishes early stands still; this tick is the operation index of Figure 7. When a run starts, the player pulls operations round robin, 2,048 at a time, until every stream ends or 60,000 operations are held in total. Every run at the default size (48 values; 3,356 operations for the default four panes) is therefore produced whole, and the scrubber's end is exact. Larger runs, up to about 159,000 operations for four quadratic sorts on 240 reversed values, continue lazily. Round robin keeps the panes' histories level, because the scrubber can reach only ticks that every still-producing pane holds. Every executed operation is kept. Seeking back replays them from the initial array, one copy per pane, instead of stepping back or resetting, and a test checks that seeking equals stepping at every tick. The costs are memory proportional to the run (recorded in the code as about 105–180 bytes per operation) and replay time for distant seeks; neither has been profiled in the browser.' Optionally add the evidence pack's Diagram 4 (docsforfyp/03_architecture_and_decisions.md lines 153-170) as a small figure.

findings.section: §4.6, paragraph 'A representative correctness issue: parallel edges'
findings.issue: p.9 presents the parallel-edge rule as a hypothetical ('Ignoring both edges during DFS can incorrectly mark one as a bridge'). It never says that this modelling choice makes VisuAlgo+ answer differently from visualgo.net on two of visualgo's own samples. When a directed sample is read undirected, VisuAlgo+ keeps its two opposite arcs as two parallel edges; visualgo.net merges them into one edge, which is then a bridge. On CP4 4.22, VisuAlgo+ reports three bridges where visualgo.net reports four; on 'Large, Cycles', 24 where it reports 25. The supervisor knows VisuAlgo's answers and may read the difference as a defect unless the report explains it. Explained, it is strong evidence of algorithmic care.

findings.fix: Rewrite the p.9 paragraph, for example: 'A modelling difference with visible consequences: parallel edges. VisuAlgo+ keeps every edge under its own id, so the two opposite arcs of a directed sample read undirected become two parallel edges. A low-link DFS must therefore skip the parent edge by id, not every edge to the parent vertex: either parallel edge can be removed without disconnecting the graph, so neither is a bridge. findings.issue: 'notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds' misstates the rule. While a run plays, a step note lasts min(1,600 ms, 0.9 × step interval), and the note is dropped when that is under 200 ms. Notes therefore disappear for steps faster than about 222 ms. Step notes pass no delay, so 'configured delay' does not apply to them. The text also omits that notes appear only when a step is reached forward, not on rewind or seek, which is a deliberate design choice worth stating.

crit-technical.notes:
Verdict: technically credible and accurately bounded, but undersold. Every technical claim I checked against 662e7b3 holds, and none oversells. What limits the score is presentation, not substance:
- no crisp contribution statement;
- decisions given without the rejected alternatives that the 95 records already state;
- tests not mapped to the risks the report names;
- a dense §4.3;
- decorative Figures 1–2 and no run-flow diagram;
- no before/after defect and no performance observation, although the repository has dated ones.

Most fixes reuse text and diagrams from the evidence pack (doc 03 Diagrams 3–4, doc 04 D2). They fit in the free space on pp. 7 and 13 (about a quarter page each) plus a slimmer Table 3 Interpretation column.

findings.issue: The system being rebuilt is described only through the 2012 paper, and selectively. (a) The 2012 paper presents VisuAlgo's predecessor and never uses the name; Halim 2015 calls VisuAlgo 'the continuation' of that work. findings.issue: The effectiveness literature is cited to draw a boundary (correctness vs learning) but is not used to justify the design, and contrary evidence is not weighed. Hundhausen et al. [3] name the learner activities that made visualizations effective, including 'constructing their own input data sets' and 'making predictions regarding future visualization states'. They report that studies in which students 'merely viewed visualizations did not demonstrate significant learning advantages', and that procedural-knowledge measures were more sensitive. Each finding bears on VisuAlgo+ (editable input, floating text as a viewing aid, the prediction tasks in Table 4), and none is used. Saraiya et al. 2004 point the other way on several VisuAlgo+ features: learner-controlled pace mattered most, a good example data set beat students' own data, and pseudocode display and stepping back showed no significant effect. A critical review should address this tension instead of treating input editing, pseudocode sync and backward seeking (§4.2) as self-evidently useful. [2]'s own student feedback is also relevant and unused: 'Visualization bugs during the early rollout affect understanding' and 'The steps shown need to be coupled with the highlight of algorithm (pseudo)codes'.

findings.fix: Replace §2.1 ¶2 with about 120 words: 'Hundhausen et al.'s meta-study of 24 experiments [3] found that how learners use a visualization matters more than what it shows. Merely viewing gave no significant advantage, while activities such as constructing one's own input or predicting the next state did. Naps et al.'s engagement taxonomy [N] grades this from viewing through responding, changing and constructing. VisuAlgo+ supports viewing and changing (editable input) but not yet responding. Saraiya et al. [S] add a caution: learner-controlled pace mattered most, a good example data set beat learners' own, and pseudocode display and stepping back showed no significant effect. This supports offering VisuAlgo's teaching examples as samples alongside editing, and it makes pseudocode synchronisation and backward seeking choices to evaluate, not established benefits. crit-literature.notes:
VERDICT (Literature Review): partially meets the criterion. Section 2 is accurate and honest: every external claim checks out against its source, and the correctness-vs-learning boundary is well drawn. But it is thin and descriptive: three peer-reviewed works, the newest from 2012, and no comparison with any system other than an OpenDSA web page. §2.3 disclaims novelty instead of positioning the work. It also leaves unused the most useful content of its own sources: Hundhausen's activity list and measurement findings, Shaffer's quality and coverage findings and his Algorithms in Action precedent, and Halim 2012's future-work agenda and student feedback. For a CA report this is a fixable weakness, not a failure. LR-2, LR-3, LR-4, LR-7 and LR-8 are text swaps inside §2 and the reference list, at the same length, doable today. LR-5 and LR-6 need the owner's answers.

PROPOSED §2 STRUCTURE (about 470 words, the same as now):
- 2.1 VisuAlgo and comparable systems (~150 words): Halim 2012's four advantages, Halim 2015's Online Quiz, what VisuAlgo+ keeps and defers (LR-3), Galles DSV, OpenDSA/JSAV (one sentence), Algorithm Visualizer (one sentence, linked to the engine boundary in §7.1).
- 2.2 What makes algorithm visualization effective (~170 words): Hundhausen (activities, viewing alone, procedural measures), the Naps taxonomy, Saraiya (pace, examples, pseudocode and stepping back), Shaffer (quality, topic skew, lost AVs), each with its consequence for VisuAlgo+ (LR-4, LR-7).
- 2.3 Position of this work (~150 words): the comparator framed by Halim 2012's own agenda; what VisuAlgo+ concentrates on; layout (VS Code) and notes (split attention) precedents in one clause each; the three design questions tied to sources (LR-2, LR-6).
- Removed to make room: the React Flow/D3 paragraph (already in §4.1 and Figure 1), both Week 10 sentences (already in §6.1), and the 'does not establish/prove' disclaimers (keep one boundary sentence). This also removes the stray words at the top of p.4.
- Optional: a compact table (system x user input / multi-topic UI / stepping back / pseudocode sync / assessment / rearrangeable layout / on-canvas notes), but only if every cell is checked on the live systems; mark unknowns '?'.

NOT CHECKED:
- The CP4101 CA rubric or any expected number of references (not on disk).
- The live visualgo.net (whether the quiz is still offered, whether the layout is fixed, whether sorting has a compare mode) and Galles DSV's playback controls. The positioning draft therefore claims nothing about what other systems lack.
- The Naps taxonomy level names (no viewing, viewing, responding, changing, constructing, presenting) are confirmed only through secondary sources; the original PDF could not be retrieved. Check before quoting.
- Saraiya et al.'s abstract was read as reproduced on bibbase.org; the ACM DL returned 403. Crossref confirms the bibliographic data.
- The EuroVis Education 2025 review (doi:10.2312/eved.20251027) resolves, but its page returned 403, so it stays 'to verify'.
- PathFinding.js exists (a grid path-finding library with a demo) but I judged it low relevance.

findings.issue:
This is a proper abstract, not a summary of limitations. It is 181 words, only one of its ten sentences is a limitation, and it gives scope, approach and concrete counts. But:
- It uses terms the reader cannot know yet: 'the V10 panel-group model', 'the audited application', '11 graph algorithm identifiers'.
- It names one feature two ways: 'short explanations placed on the drawing' and 'floating text on the canvas'.
- One sentence just lists contents ('This report explains…'), and one is vague ('These results support functional progress').
findings.evidence: main.tex:51; computed word count 181. For comparison, the final-report format (not binding for CA) asks for at most 200 words.
findings.fix: Replace 'the V10 panel-group model' with 'a shared layout of movable panel groups around a fixed canvas (V10)', 'audited application' with 'current application', and 'algorithm identifiers' with 'algorithms'. Use 'floating text' in both places. Turn the contents sentence into contributions (e.g. 'I separated input, layout and playback state, built a tested panel-layout model…'). Delete 'These results support functional progress.'

positives: The structure maps onto the official CA items: objectives (§1.3), related work (§2), progress (§3-5), plan (§6.3-7) and references.
The abstract is a real abstract: 181 words, one limitation sentence out of ten, with concrete counts. Putting it on the cover saves a page.
The TikZ diagrams (Figures 1-2) are vector, legible at caption size, and their captions explain the dashed elements. Keep them as they are.
Figure 8's caption quotes the on-screen note (4 + 3 < 8, so E goes from 8 to 7). It is the model for the other captions.
Table 2's 'Example consequence' column and Table 5's 'Completion evidence' column make design and plan items concrete and checkable.
Concrete examples explain design choices to a newcomer: moving vertex B versus changing an edge weight, and parallel edges versus the parent-edge rule.
Conventions are consistent: 'Week 10' is capitalized in all 12 uses, spelling is Oxford-style throughout (behaviour, colour, catalogue, -ize), and en dashes are used correctly (Bellman–Ford, 15–20).
The LaTeX source is self-contained and reproducible: a scratch rebuild produced the submitted PDF exactly (16 pages, 1,470,513 bytes).
The AI-use disclosure is one paragraph on p5, and the contribution split in §3.2 is stated plainly. Keep both.
§6.2 works well as the single home for evidence boundaries. Once the repeats elsewhere are cut, it carries the caveats on its own.

C. LIVE DEMO: 'Dijkstra on the default /sssp graph', about 4 minutes. It shows a dead step and an update explained on the canvas, a drag that keeps the run, an edit that ends it, and a panel move that persists. Rehearse it once.

confirmed.issue:
The timing paragraph is wrong in three places.
1. 'Notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds': the 200 ms floor applies to the note's remaining display time, which is 90% of the step interval. A 200 ms step therefore gets no note; the first interval that shows one is about 223 ms.
2. 'Limited by the step interval and configured delay': step notes have no delay, because the writer always sets delayMs to 0. The only setting involved is Speed, which together with the step's pace gives the interval.
3. 'A manually inspected note': notes appear only when a step is reached one step forward (Next or autoplay). Previous, First, Last and the scrubber show none.

This matters for the section's own example. At the default 0.5 s speed during autoplay, a rejected Dijkstra relaxation ('· keep') note shows for about 0.3 s, and an 'already settled' note does not show at all.
confirmed.evidence:
- prototypes/src/shared/visualization/floatingTextTiming.ts:11, :13 and :27-30: durationMs is min(1600, 0.9 × effectiveIntervalMs − delayMs) while playing and 1600 otherwise; it is undefined below 200 ms.

- shared/visualization/stepNotes.ts:43-48: no note unless arrival.forward; delayMs is 0. useStepArrival.ts:5-10 defines 'forward'.
- graph/visualization/sessionReducer.ts:5: default interval 500 ms. graph/visualization/playbackTiming.ts:15-23: pace multipliers.
- graph/algorithms/dijkstra/playbackTiming.ts:20-31: an update uses 'emphasis' (1,000 ms), a keep uses 'fast' (350 ms), a settled target uses 'very-fast' (200 ms).
- DD-61, docs/graph/DESIGN_DECISIONS.md:2699-2710, and the DD-17 row at line 29 say the same: 'a keep's 0.315s', and a settled target's note 'shows while playing only from 0.60 s per frame'.

After Next it lasts 1,600 ms; during autoplay it is cut to 90% of the step's interval (Speed × the step's pace) and omitted when less than 200 ms would remain. At the default 0.5 s speed, a Dijkstra update's note shows for 0.9 s, a kept relaxation's for about 0.3 s, and an already-settled note not at all.' confirmed.verify_reason:
I reproduced all three errors.
- Threshold: while playing, a note lasts min(1600, 0.9 × interval − delay) ms and is dropped below 200 ms (floatingTextTiming.ts:28-29). The test at :29-30 gives 223 ms → 201 and 200 ms → none, so the cut-off is about 222 ms of step interval, not 200.
- Delay: notes have none; delayMs is always 0 (stepNotes.ts:48).
- Backward moves: a note shows only after a one-step-forward move (stepNotes.ts:44), so Previous, First, Last and the scrubber show none.
The interval is Speed × the step's pace (useVisualizationSession.ts:105; multipliers in playbackTiming.ts:15-23; Dijkstra paces in dijkstra/playbackTiming.ts:20-31; default 500 ms in sessionReducer.ts:5). The DD-17 row (graph DD:29) and DD-61 (:2697-2710) give 0.9 s for an update, 0.315 s for a keep and nothing for a settled target at the default speed. The section's own example, a kept relaxation, is therefore the shortest-lived note in default autoplay, and a settled target gets none. Doc 02:122 states the rule correctly; the errors come from the report's paraphrase.

confirmed.issue: The effectiveness literature is cited to draw a boundary (correctness vs learning) but is not used to justify the design, and contrary evidence is not weighed. Hundhausen et al. confirmed.section: 4.8 Floating text: explanations on the canvas (timing paragraph)
confirmed.issue: MISMATCH: 'During autoplay, its duration is limited by the step interval and configured delay; notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds' misstates the code. During autoplay a note lasts min(1,600 ms, 0.9 x step interval - delay), and it is dropped when that result is under 200 ms. Step notes are always created with delay 0, so they disappear when the step interval is below about 222 ms, not 200 ms, and no configured delay applies to them. The evidence pack states this correctly (doc 02 line 122); the report's paraphrase lost the 0.9 factor. The 1,600 ms life when stepping by hand is a MATCH.
confirmed.evidence: visualgo-plus-design@662e7b3: prototypes/src/shared/visualization/floatingTextTiming.ts:11 (FLOATING_NOTE_MS = 1600), :13 (FLOATING_TEXT_MIN_MS = 200), :27-29 (cutToStep: Math.min(lifeMs, effectiveIntervalMs * 0.9 - delayMs); undefined when < 200). prototypes/src/shared/visualization/stepNotes.ts:45 (floatingNoteDurationMs(arrival), called with no delay) and :48 (delayMs: 0). floatingTextTiming.test.ts:22 (1000 ms interval -> 900 ms), :29 (223 ms -> 201 ms, shown), :30 (200 ms -> none). docsforfyp/02_contribution_evidence.md:122.
confirmed.fix: Replace the two sentences with: 'When the learner steps forward by hand, a note lasts 1,600 milliseconds. During autoplay it is cut to 90% of the step interval and left out when less than 200 milliseconds would remain (steps shorter than about 222 milliseconds).' Delete 'and configured delay'.
confirmed.verify_reason: I reproduced this in the code. floatingTextTiming.ts:27-29 sets a note's autoplay life to min(1600, 0.9 x effectiveIntervalMs - delay) and drops the note when that is under 200 ms. stepNotes.ts:45 and :48 always pass a delay of 0, so text notes disappear for step intervals below about 222 ms, not 200 ms. The test at floatingTextTiming.test.ts:29 shows a 223 ms interval giving a 201 ms note, and :30 shows 200 ms giving none. The band is reachable: the graph's minimum interval is 50 ms (graph/visualization/sessionReducer.ts:3). Only the segment-tree number popups pass a delay (tree/algorithms/segment/valuePopups.ts:91). confirmed.issue: The sorting limitation sentence is wrong in two ways. (1) History is never trimmed, but it is not unbounded: every input is capped at 240 values, and a code comment records the worst-case size. (2) 'Distant seeks can require substantial replay' gets the cost model wrong. A backward seek always replays from a fresh state up to the target, so its cost grows with the target's position, not with how far the seek jumps. In addition, at the app's input sizes the 60,000-operation priming usually holds the whole comparison, so the lazy path only matters for the largest combinations.
confirmed.evidence: docsforfyp report/main.tex:195, and :312 ('Sorting retains unbounded history'). visualgo-plus-design prototypes/src/sorting/app/useSortingExperiment.ts:25 sets MAX_CUSTOM_VALUES = 240, enforced on the resolved input at :90-91. Bao's comment above EAGER_OPERATION_CAP (src/sorting/comparison/operationBuffer.ts:232-246, from 5ccef45) records counts: shipped 4-pane default at n=48 = 3,356 operations; n=160 = 25,015; n=240 = 53,034; worst 4-pane choice at n=240 = 159,298; 105-180 bytes per operation. Priming runs to 60,000 summed across panes (:292-327). For a backward seek, seekComparison calls replayOperations(input, run.history.slice(0, consumed)) (src/sorting/comparison/comparisonPlayback.ts:346-352). replayOperations is applySortOperations(createPlaybackState(input), operations) (src/sorting/engine/operations.ts:446-451). A one-step Previous instead reverts a single operation (retreatComparison, comparisonPlayback.ts:257-300).
confirmed.fix: In main.tex:195, replace the second sentence with: 'However, retained history is never trimmed (only the 240-value input cap bounds it), and a backward seek replays the retained operations from the start up to the target, so its cost grows with how late the target lies rather than with the distance jumped.' main.tex:312 can keep 'unbounded' or read 'never trims its history'.
confirmed.verify_reason: Seek cost: reproduced. A backward seekComparison replays from a fresh state via replayOperations(input, run.history.slice(0, consumed)) (comparisonPlayback.ts:346-352; engine/operations.ts:446-451). Its cost therefore grows with the target's position, not with how far the seek jumps; a forward seek is a batch advance and Previous reverts one operation (:257-300). 'Unbounded': overstated as an error. The project's own records use that word for never-trimmed history (prototypes/docs/sorting/IMPROVEMENT_BACKLOG.md:61-63; sorting-performance-milestone.md:139), and the 240-value cap (useSortingExperiment.ts:25, 90-91) bounds it in practice. Stating that bound adds precision; it does not correct an error. Drop the colleague's 'priming usually holds the whole comparison' clause: whether it holds depends on the algorithm mix (worst four-pane case 159,298 operations against a 60,000 cap), so it adds a claim nobody has tested.

confirmed.issue: 'notes are suppressed for intervals below 200 milliseconds' is not the rule in the code. confirmed.verify_reason: Reproduced, and the error is wider than stated. floatingTextTiming.ts:27-30 cuts a note during playback to min(1600, 0.9 × interval − delay) and drops it below 200 ms. stepNotes.ts:44-49 passes a delay of 0, so notes have no 'configured delay' and disappear at intervals below about 222 ms.
